title: US Immigration Curbs Could Cost Economy $668 Billion, Study Estimates
excerpt: An NFAP analysis estimates a 20% fall in international STEM graduate students could cost the U.S. $668 billion a year in patent-linked value, while research it reviews finds H-1B restrictions push firms to expand employment in India and other countries.
body:
• A National Foundation for American Policy study published November 2 estimates a 20% decrease in international STEM graduate students could cost the U.S. economy $668 billion a year — an estimate, not a measured loss.
  • The same analysis says a 20% increase would add $668 billion a year, based on the value of patents linked to foreign STEM graduate students enrolled in fall 2024.
  • Research reviewed in the study finds H-1B restrictions push firms to increase employment abroad, particularly in China, India and Canada, with research and development jobs most affected.
  • No rule changes in this study: there is no new fee, deadline or filing step for applicants — the practical step is to check current requirements before any filing and watch for policy proposals.

Stricter U.S. immigration rules for skilled workers and students could push more work to India and other countries, according to a study published on November 2 by the National Foundation for American Policy (NFAP). The study, The Economic Contributions of High-Skilled Immigration, combines original NFAP research with a review of the economic literature, and concludes that the United States would benefit from increasing, not reducing, the entry of foreign-born talent.

NFAP does not say the economy has lost $668 billion. It estimates what a large fall in international student numbers could cost each year — and what a large rise could add.

Who is affected — exactly

The groups at the centre of the study are international STEM graduate students, H-1B visa holders and their employers, and the U.S.-born workers alongside them. India is specifically named in the offshoring research the study cites. The study announces no new restriction and changes nothing for anyone with an existing visa, pending application or university place.

What the $668 billion figure actually says

The figure comes from an NFAP analysis of research by economists Gnanaraj Chellaraj of the World Bank, Keith E. Maskus of the University of Colorado and Aaditya Mattoo of the World Bank. According to that research, an additional foreign STEM graduate student results in 0.57 patents granted. Based on the value of patents and the number of STEM international graduate students enrolled in the United States in fall 2024, NFAP calculates that a 10% increase in enrolled STEM international graduate students would add $334 billion to the U.S. economy each year, and a 20% increase would add $668 billion a year.

Run in the other direction, NFAP says a 10% decrease in international graduate students in science and engineering could cost the U.S. economy $334 billion a year, and a 20% decrease could cost $668 billion. Both directions are modelled estimates built on patent values. They are not forecasts that student numbers will fall by 20%, and they are not a count of money already lost.

Why the study says jobs move to India

The offshoring finding rests on separate research the brief reviews. Britta Glennon, an assistant professor at the Wharton School of the University of Pennsylvania, found that firms respond to restrictions on H-1B immigration by increasing foreign affiliate employment, particularly in China, India and Canada, and that research and development jobs were most affected. The brief quotes her conclusion that policies aimed at reducing immigration can have, in her words, the unintended consequence of encouraging firms to offshore jobs abroad.

Economists Giovanni Peri, Kevin Shih, Chad Sparber and Angie Marek Zeitlin found that jobs for U.S.-born workers in computer-related industries would have grown at least 55% faster between 2005-2006 and 2009-2010 if not for the denial of so many H-1B applications in the visa lotteries. NFAP extrapolates from petition numbers USCIS rejected because of the annual limit in fiscal 2024 and 2025 to estimate that up to 615,000 more jobs for U.S.-born technology workers could have been created with a higher limit. That, too, is an extrapolation, not a hiring count.

What else the study reports

NFAP reports that immigrants founded or cofounded 59% of America's privately held startup companies valued at $1 billion or more — 455 of 775 companies — and that about 24% of U.S. billion-dollar companies have a founder who came to America as an international student. It also cites research attributing between 30% and 50% of U.S. aggregate productivity growth between 1990 and 2010 to inflows of foreign STEM workers. NFAP Executive Director Stuart Anderson said, in the study's release summary, that the consensus among economists is that immigrants, international students and H-1B visa holders contribute significantly to the U.S. economy.

When, and what to do next

There is no effective date or deadline in this study. It is evidence in a policy argument, not a rule. For a student weighing a U.S. STEM application or a worker weighing an H-1B-sponsored move, the study changes none of the current requirements; the correct action is to check the current official requirements for the specific visa or university route before filing or paying anything, and to treat proposals reported elsewhere as proposals until an agency publishes a final rule. What to watch is whether Congress or the administration moves on the annual H-1B limit, student routes or green card exemptions — the brief cites a research estimate that exempting STEM master's and Ph.D. holders from green card limits could cut the federal deficit by $634 billion over 20 years, not a scored bill.
